items.stem: A cell shows 1,250 but SUM ignores it and other obviously numeric cells. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The numbers are stored as text, so SUM does not add them
options.rationale: Correct: text that looks numeric is excluded by SUM; convert it to a number to fix the total.

options.text: Excel can only SUM up to 100 cells
options.rationale: There is no such limit; SUM handles very large ranges.

options.text: The AVERAGE function is interfering with SUM
options.rationale: Functions do not interfere with each other this way.
Formatting changes appearance only, not whether a value is numeric.

items.explanation: Correct: text that looks numeric is excluded by SUM; convert it to a number to fix the total.

items.stem: You copied =B2*C2 down a column but every row multiplies by the same tax rate in C2. Which TWO fixes make it copy correctly? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Lock the rate with an absolute reference, e.g. =B2*$C$2
options.rationale: Correct: anchoring the rate keeps it fixed while B adjusts per row.

options.text: Put the rate in the formula as a typed number repeated per row
options.rationale: Correct: hard-coding the same rate per row also yields correct results, though it is less maintainable.
The fill handle is a tool, not the cause of the error.
Formatting does not change which cell a reference points to.

items.explanation: Correct: anchoring the rate keeps it fixed while B adjusts per row.

items.stem: Which action changes only how a value looks, not the value Excel stores?

options.text: Applying a number format such as currency or percentage
options.rationale: Correct: number formats affect display only; the underlying value is unchanged.

options.text: Typing a new number into the cell

options.rationale: ROUND changes the computed value, not just its display.
